23115:
Shepherds kept flocks of sheep and goats, leading them to pasture and water, guarding them from predators and thieves, and folding them at night. Israel's ancestors were semi-nomadic herders, and the Bible's leaders are repeatedly drawn from the sheepfold: Abel, Jacob, Rachel, Moses and David all kept flocks.

The work was demanding and often solitary. Jacob describes heat by day, frost by night and personal liability for lost animals, and David speaks of fighting a lion and a bear to rescue a lamb.
23122: God is pictured as Israel's shepherd who leads, provides and protects, the basis of Psalm 23.
23123: Ezekiel condemns Israel's leaders as shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock and promises that God himself, through a Davidic shepherd, will tend his sheep.
23124: Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who knows his sheep and lays down his life for them.
23125: The parable of the lost sheep shows God's joy over one sinner who repents.
23126: Shepherds keeping watch at night are the first to hear the announcement of the Messiah's birth.
23127:
Most Israelites were subsistence farmers growing wheat, barley, olives, grapes and figs on family plots held as an inheritance from God. The agricultural year ran from ploughing and sowing with the early rains in autumn, through the barley harvest around Passover and the wheat harvest around Pentecost, to the grape and olive harvests at the Feast of Booths.

The law built care for the poor into farming: field corners and gleanings were left for the poor, the foreigner, the widow and the orphan, as Ruth's gleaning in Boaz's field shows.
23135: The parable of the sower explains different responses to God's word through different kinds of soil.
23136: The seed growing secretly and the mustard seed picture the kingdom's hidden, God-given growth.
23137: Putting a hand to the plough and looking back illustrates divided discipleship.
23138: John the Baptist describes the coming judge winnowing wheat from chaff.
23139: Paul says one planted, another watered, but God gives the growth, and that a person reaps what they sow.
23140: A grain of wheat must fall into the ground and die to bear much fruit, an image of Jesus' death.
23141:
Vinedressers planted, pruned and protected vineyards, clearing stones, building a hedge or wall and a watchtower, and cutting a winepress into the rock. Vineyards took years to become productive, so planting one was an act of long-term hope; the law even exempted a man who had planted a vineyard but not yet enjoyed it from war.

When Babylon deported Judah's elite, the poorest of the land were left behind to be vinedressers and farmers.
23147: Isaiah's song of the vineyard pictures Israel as a carefully tended vine that produced only wild grapes.
23148: Jesus is the true vine, his Father the vinedresser who prunes fruitful branches.
23149: The parable of the wicked tenants recalls Isaiah's vineyard and indicts Israel's leaders.
23150: In the parable of the labourers in the vineyard, the owner pays latecomers the same wage, showing grace rather than merit.
23151: A vinedresser pleads for one more year for a barren fig tree, a picture of patient but limited mercy.
23152: Beating swords into pruning hooks is the prophetic image of universal peace.
23153:
Fishing on the Sea of Galilee was a significant industry. Fishermen worked at night with casting nets, dragnets and trammel nets, sorted the catch on shore, and mended and washed their nets. Fish were salted and dried for trade; Magdala was a known fish-processing town.

At least four of Jesus' first disciples were fishermen: the brothers Peter and Andrew, and the brothers James and John, whose father Zebedee had hired servants, suggesting a modest family business. Peter and Andrew appear to have worked in partnership with them.
23156: Wooden boat with oars and sail
23159: Jesus calls fishermen to become fishers of people.
23160: The parable of the dragnet pictures final judgment sorting good from bad.
23161: Jeremiah uses fishers and hunters as an image of God gathering his people, and Ezekiel pictures fishermen on the restored river from the temple.
23162: The risen Jesus repeats the miraculous catch and restores Peter beside a charcoal fire.
23163: Peter pays the temple tax with a coin from the mouth of a fish caught by hook.
23164:
Luke says Paul, Aquila and Priscilla were tentmakers (Greek *skēnopoioi*). Whether this meant working leather, goat-hair cloth from Paul's native Cilicia, or linen for awnings is debated; most scholars think leatherwork is likely. The trade was portable, so a craftsman could set up shop in any city's market.

Paul worked with his own hands so as not to burden his churches, though he insisted that preachers had a right to support. The modern phrase "tentmaking ministry" for self-supporting mission comes from his example.
23170: Paul worked night and day to avoid being a burden and to give an example of diligence.
23171: Paul defends his right to support but chooses not to use it for the gospel's sake.
23172: The body is pictured as an earthly tent to be exchanged for a building from God.
23173: John says the Word became flesh and pitched his tent (dwelt) among us, echoing the tabernacle.
23174:
In first-century Judea and Galilee, tolls and customs were farmed out to contractors who bid for the right to collect them and kept what they gathered above the contracted sum. Matthew (Levi) sat at a toll booth in Capernaum; Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector in Jericho, a major customs point on the trade route.

The system invited extortion. John the Baptist told tax collectors to collect no more than authorised, and Zacchaeus promised fourfold restitution to anyone he had defrauded.
23179: In the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector, the one who beats his breast and asks for mercy goes home justified.
23180: Jesus eats with tax collectors, saying he came to call sinners, not the righteous.
23181: Tax collectors and prostitutes enter the kingdom ahead of the religious leaders because they believed John.
23182: Zacchaeus' restitution shows salvation reaching a house, for the Son of Man came to seek and save the lost.
23183:
Scribes were trained writers who drafted letters, contracts and royal records, copied sacred texts and, increasingly, interpreted them. In the monarchy, royal scribes such as Shaphan were senior officials. Baruch wrote down Jeremiah's oracles, and Ezra is called a scribe skilled in the law of Moses.

By the time of Jesus, "scribes" (grammateis) were experts in the law, many associated with the Pharisees, and some sat on the Sanhedrin. The Gospels show them both opposing Jesus and, in one case, being "not far from the kingdom of God."
23189: A scribe trained for the kingdom brings out of his treasure things new and old.
23190: Jesus warns against scribes who love honour and devour widows' houses.
23191: A scribe who grasps that love of God and neighbour outweighs sacrifices is told he is not far from the kingdom.
23192: God promises to write his law on hearts, and Paul calls the church a letter written by the Spirit.
23193:
Potters shaped clay on a wheel turned by hand or foot, then fired the vessels in a kiln. Pottery was cheap, everywhere and easily broken, which is why archaeologists date sites by their potsherds. Jars, lamps, cooking pots and storage vessels were all ceramic.

Jeremiah watched a potter rework a spoiled vessel and was told that God can do the same with a nation; he later smashed a clay flask to signify Jerusalem's irreparable judgment.
23199: God as potter has the right to reshape the clay; repentance or rebellion changes what he does.
23200: The clay may not question the potter, an image of creaturely humility.
23201: The gospel treasure is held in fragile clay jars to show the power belongs to God.
23202: Judas' thirty pieces of silver bought the potter's field, linked by Matthew to prophecy.
23204:
Joseph is called a *tektōn* and so is Jesus himself. The Greek word means a craftsman or builder, usually in wood but sometimes in stone or metal; "carpenter" is the traditional English rendering, but "builder" or "craftsman" may be closer. A village tektōn might make doors, ploughs, yokes and furniture and help build houses.

Justin Martyr in the second century says Jesus made ploughs and yokes. Some scholars suggest Joseph and Jesus could have found work at nearby Sepphoris, rebuilt by Herod Antipas, but the Gospels say nothing of it.
23211: The wise man builds his house on rock, the foolish on sand.
23212: Count the cost before building a tower, as one must before following Jesus.
23213: Jesus offers an easy yoke and light burden, perhaps drawing on a craftsman's knowledge of well-fitted yokes.
23214: The rejected stone becomes the cornerstone, and the church is built on the foundation of apostles and prophets.
23215: Paul as a skilled master builder laid the foundation, which is Jesus Christ; each worker's building will be tested.
23216: Amos' plumb line tests whether Israel is upright.
23217:
Merchants moved goods by caravan and ship: grain, oil, wine, metals, spices, textiles and luxury items. Canaan sat on routes linking Egypt, Arabia and Mesopotamia, and Phoenician Tyre ran a Mediterranean trading network that Ezekiel describes in detail. Solomon profited from horse and chariot trade and from Red Sea voyages.

In the New Testament Lydia trades in purple cloth, and Revelation's lament over Babylon is voiced partly by merchants who grew rich from her.
23223: A merchant sells everything for one pearl of great value, as the kingdom is worth everything.
23224: The parable of the talents commends faithful investment of what the master entrusts.
23225: False balances are an abomination, and the prophets attack merchants who cheat the poor.
23226: James warns traders who plan profits without saying "if the Lord wills."
23227: Merchants weep over Babylon's fall, whose cargo list ends with human souls.
23228:
Early Israel fought with tribal militias summoned in crisis. Saul began, and David expanded, a standing professional force, with commanders such as Joab and elite warriors called the Mighty Men, among them foreign mercenaries such as Uriah the Hittite.

In the New Testament, Roman soldiers and centurions (officers over roughly eighty to a hundred men) appear frequently. Several are portrayed positively: the centurion at Capernaum, the centurion at the cross, and Cornelius at Caesarea.
23234: John the Baptist tells soldiers not to extort and to be content with their wages.
23235: A centurion's faith in Jesus' authority is praised above any found in Israel.
23236: Paul describes the armour of God for spiritual conflict.
23237: Timothy is to share suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus, not entangled in civilian affairs.
23238: The centurion at the cross confesses Jesus as Son of God.
23239:
Ancient physicians used herbal remedies, oils, wine, poultices and bandages, set bones and dressed wounds. Egypt had renowned physicians, who embalmed Jacob. Israel's priests did not practise medicine as such, but they inspected skin diseases and declared people clean.

Paul calls Luke "the beloved physician." Older scholars argued that Luke's vocabulary is distinctively medical; that argument is now generally thought weak, since educated Greek writers used similar terms, but the identification of Luke as a physician rests on Colossians, not on vocabulary.
23245: Jesus says the healthy do not need a physician but the sick, explaining his mission to sinners.
23246: "Physician, heal yourself" is the proverb Jesus anticipates at Nazareth.
23247: Jeremiah asks whether there is no balm in Gilead, lamenting a people who will not be healed.
23248: The Good Samaritan treats wounds with oil and wine.
23249: The LORD presents himself as Israel's healer.
23251:
Smiths worked bronze, iron, silver and gold, smelting ore, refining in a crucible and hammering or casting tools, weapons and ornaments. Genesis names Tubal-cain as the forger of bronze and iron tools. Under Saul the Philistines held a monopoly on ironworking and Israelites had to go to them to sharpen tools.

Hiram of Tyre cast the bronze pillars and vessels for Solomon's temple. In Acts, Demetrius the silversmith stirs a riot in Ephesus because Paul's preaching threatened the trade in silver shrines of Artemis.
23257: God is like a refiner's fire and a fuller's soap, purifying his people like silver.
23258: The crucible is for silver and the furnace for gold, but the LORD tests hearts.
23259: Faith tested by trials is more precious than gold refined by fire.
23260: Isaiah mocks the smith who forges an idol and grows tired.
23261: Swords will be beaten into ploughshares in the age of peace.
23263:
Genesis names Jubal as the ancestor of lyre and pipe players. Miriam led the women with tambourines after the Red Sea crossing, and David was known as a skilled lyre player whose music eased Saul's torment.

Chronicles describes David organising Levitical families, under Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, as temple singers and instrumentalists, some said to "prophesy" with lyres, harps and cymbals. Many psalms carry headings naming these guilds.
23271: Believers are to speak to one another in psalms, hymns and spiritual songs.
23272: Without love, even inspired speech is a noisy gong or clanging cymbal.
23273: Paul compares unintelligible tongues to an indistinct trumpet call.
23274: Jesus compares his generation to children who will neither dance to the flute nor mourn to a dirge.
23275: Heaven's worship includes harps and a new song to the Lamb.
23276:
Spinning and weaving were household work in Israel, done largely by women with a spindle, distaff and upright loom; skilled weavers and embroiderers made the tabernacle hangings. Dyeing produced blue, purple and scarlet. True purple from murex shellfish was very expensive and associated with royalty; cheaper plant-based purples also existed.

Lydia of Thyatira, "a seller of purple" in Philippi, was likely a merchant of dyed cloth; inscriptions attest dyers' guilds at Thyatira. Dorcas in Joppa made tunics and garments for widows.
23281: Murex shell or plant dyes (madder, indigo)
23282: The capable wife works wool and flax, holds the distaff and clothes her household in scarlet.
23283: Job says his days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle; Hezekiah says his life is rolled up like a weaver's cloth.
23284: Sins as scarlet will be made white as snow, a dyer's image of cleansing.
23285: The psalmist says God knit him together in his mother's womb.
23286: Jesus' seamless tunic, woven in one piece, was gambled for at the cross.
23287:
Tanners turned animal hides into leather by scraping, soaking in lime and tanning with bark or other agents. The process was foul-smelling and used animal carcasses and dung, so tanneries were usually set at the edge of towns and, where possible, near water.

Peter stayed "many days" with Simon, a tanner whose house was by the sea in Joppa, and it was on Simon's roof that he saw the vision of clean and unclean animals before going to Cornelius. Many interpreters see significance in Peter lodging with a man whose work involved constant contact with dead animals.
23292: The vision of the sheet with unclean animals, received at a tanner's house, prepares Peter to welcome Gentiles.
23293: New wine needs new wineskins, a leather image for the newness of Jesus' ministry.
23294: Elijah and John the Baptist both wore leather belts, marking prophetic austerity.
23296:
In the Good Samaritan parable, the wounded man is taken to an inn (*pandocheion*) and the Samaritan pays the innkeeper to care for him. Such roadside lodgings offered shelter for travellers and animals but had a poor reputation.

The word in Luke 2:7, traditionally "inn," is *katalyma*, the same word used for the "guest room" of the Last Supper; many scholars now read it as a family guest room rather than a commercial inn, though the traditional reading still has defenders. Some Jewish tradition and the historian Josephus describe Rahab as an innkeeper rather than a prostitute, though the Hebrew word normally means prostitute.
23301: The Samaritan entrusts the injured man to an innkeeper and promises to repay any extra cost, showing costly neighbour-love.
23302: There was no room in the katalyma, so the newborn was laid in a manger.
23303: Believers are urged to show hospitality to strangers, as some have entertained angels unaware.
23305:
Large households were run by servants and slaves, and a steward (Greek *oikonomos*) managed the master's property, accounts and staff. Joseph became overseer of Potiphar's house and later of all Egypt; Abraham's chief servant ran his household. In the Roman world many stewards were themselves slaves.

Slavery in the ancient world differed from race-based chattel slavery but was still ownership of persons. Paul's letter to Philemon concerns Onesimus, a slave who had become a believer.
23310: The faithful and wise steward is set over the household; the one who abuses his position is judged.
23311: The shrewd steward is commended for foresight, not dishonesty, as a lesson in using wealth for eternal ends.
23312: Apostles are servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries, required above all to be faithful.
23313: Each believer is a steward of God's varied grace.
23314: Jesus came not to be served but to serve and give his life as a ransom.
23316:
Perfumers (Hebrew *raqqach*) blended spices, resins and oils into ointments and incense. The law specified the holy anointing oil and incense "after the art of the perfumer," and Nehemiah lists a perfumer among those who rebuilt the wall.

Costly ointments such as nard were stored in alabaster flasks. Mary of Bethany anointed Jesus with a pound of pure nard, and Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea used about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes in his burial.
23319: Spices and resins (myrrh, frankincense, nard, cinnamon)
23322: The anointing at Bethany is praised as preparing Jesus' body for burial.
23323: Believers are the aroma of Christ, a fragrance of life to some and death to others.
23324: Christ's self-offering is a fragrant sacrifice to God.
23325: Dead flies make the perfumer's ointment stink, as a little folly outweighs wisdom.
23327:
Hunting supplemented diet and protected flocks. Genesis calls Nimrod a mighty hunter and describes Esau as a skilful hunter, a man of the field, in contrast to Jacob who stayed among the tents. Isaac loved Esau's game, which set up the stolen blessing.

Fowlers caught birds with nets, snares and traps, and the image of the snare is common in psalms and wisdom literature.
23332: God delivers from the snare of the fowler.
23333: A person caught by a rash pledge should free himself like a gazelle from the hunter.
23334: Amos asks whether a bird falls into a trap with no bait, arguing that disaster has a cause.
23335: Jeremiah pictures God sending fishers and hunters to search out his people.
23337:
Israel was not a seafaring nation; its coast had few natural harbours, and the sea often symbolised chaos. Solomon and Jehoshaphat used Phoenician expertise for Red Sea voyages. Jonah sailed from Joppa on a ship whose crew feared the storm, prayed to their gods and finally to the LORD.

Acts 27 gives one of the most detailed ancient accounts of a voyage and shipwreck, including sounding the depth, dropping anchors from the stern and lightening the ship.
23343: Those who go down to the sea in ships see God's wonders and cry out to him in the storm.
23344: A small rudder steers a great ship, as the tongue directs a life.
23345: Hope is an anchor for the soul.
23346: Some have made shipwreck of their faith.
23347: Jesus calms the storm on the Sea of Galilee, displaying authority over the sea.
23349:
A cupbearer served wine to the king and was responsible for making sure it was safe, so the post required complete trust. Pharaoh's chief cupbearer was imprisoned with Joseph and later remembered him. The Queen of Sheba was impressed by Solomon's cupbearers.

Nehemiah was cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes I. His access to the king allowed him to request leave, letters and timber to rebuild Jerusalem's walls.
23353: The cup can symbolise God's wrath or his salvation.
23354: Jesus prays for the cup to pass from him, yet submits to the Father's will.
23355: The cup of the Lord's Supper is the new covenant in Jesus' blood.
23356: Nehemiah prays silently before answering the king, a model of courage in a position of service.
23357:
Israel's priests were descendants of Aaron within the tribe of Levi. They offered sacrifices, burned incense, kept the lamps, blessed the people, judged matters of ritual purity and taught the law. The high priest alone entered the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement.

Before Sinai, Melchizedek and Jethro appear as priests outside Israel. Several prophets were from priestly families, including Jeremiah and Ezekiel. In the New Testament era the high priesthood was politically appointed, and Annas and Caiaphas presided over Jesus' hearings.

The New Testament presents Jesus as the great high priest after the order of Melchizedek and calls the church a royal priesthood. Traditions differ on whether Christian ministers are priests in a sacramental sense (Catholic, Orthodox) or whether priesthood belongs to all believers with no distinct sacerdotal order (most Protestants).
23364: Israel as a whole was to be a kingdom of priests, and the church is called a royal priesthood.
23365: Jesus is the high priest who sympathises with weakness and offered himself once for all.
23366: The lips of a priest should guard knowledge, for he is the LORD's messenger.
23367: In the Good Samaritan parable a priest passes by on the other side.
23368: Paul describes his gospel work as priestly service offering the Gentiles to God.
23369:
The tribe of Levi was set apart for sacred service after its zeal at the golden calf. Levites who were not descendants of Aaron assisted the priests: carrying and guarding the tabernacle, later serving as temple gatekeepers, singers, treasurers and teachers of the law.

Levites received no tribal territory. Instead they lived in forty-eight towns scattered across Israel and were supported by tithes, so that the LORD was their inheritance. Moses, Aaron and Miriam were Levites, as was Barnabas in the New Testament.
23370: Carrying poles for the ark and furnishings
23374: The LORD himself is the Levites' inheritance, a model for finding one's portion in God rather than property.
23375: Levites helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it.
23376: In the Good Samaritan parable a Levite also passes by.
